title: When Ugly Websites Actually Work
subtitle: Why users under 30 love the web’s rawest, strangest designs, and why their parents can’t stand them.
html:
For my thesis, I spent months staring at websites most people would call ugly, broken, or straight-up annoying. The twist? A lot of users under 30 actually liked them. Older users? Not so much. It turns out ‘bad design’ might just be design meant for someone else.

My research looked at brutalism in web design, that raw, stripped-down style with blocky typography, strange layouts, weird cursors and almost no decoration. It’s the opposite of the smooth, rounded, pastel websites we’re used to. The name comes from brutalist architecture: bare concrete, no polish, function on display. On the web, it shows up in two flavors. There’s L’Internet Brut, the clean and minimal kind, and L’Internet Fou, the chaotic kind that deliberately breaks every UX rule in the book.

To see how real people cope with these sites, I ran a study with 34 participants split into two age groups: 18-30 and 31-45. Each person tried four brutalist websites, two online shops and two informational sites, on both desktop and mobile. I measured where they clicked first, whether they completed the task, and how they rated the experience using the standard System Usability Scale.

The results were pretty clear. Younger users handled brutalism surprisingly well; on one of the shops they hit a 100% first-click success rate and gave satisfaction scores above 80. Older users struggled, especially with the chaotic Fou style, where success rates on the informational site dropped below 10%.

My conclusion: brutalism isn’t bad design, it’s targeted design. It can work beautifully for cultural, creative or fashion-oriented brands aiming at a younger audience, but if your users expect buttons where buttons normally go, keeping a visible grid and a normal cursor goes a long way. Rawness sells, as long as it doesn’t ask too much of the person looking at it.
